passages.original: Sit nunc aliunde res, ne Poenicum inter Romanos aut erubescat aut doleat. Certe habitum vertere naturae totius sollemne munus est. Fungitur et ipse mundus interim iste quem incumbimus. Viderit Anaximander, si plures putat, viderit, si quis uspiam alius, ad Meropas, ut Silenus penes aures Midae blatit, aptas sane grandioribus fabulis. Sed et si quem Plato aestimat, cuius imago hic sit, etiam ille habeat necesse est proinde mutare.
passages.english: Now let the matter be taken from elsewhere, so that what is Punic may not either blush or grieve among Romans. Certainly, to change one's dress is the customary function of all nature. Even this very world which we occupy performs it all the while. Let Anaximander see to it, if he thinks there are more [worlds]; let anyone else see to it, if there is [another world] anywhere, among the Meropes, as Silenus babbles in the ears of Midas, ears well suited indeed to taller tales. But even if Plato reckons there is some [world] of which this one is the image, that one too must likewise change.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is obscure: 'Sit nunc aliunde res' seems to mean 'let the argument now begin from another quarter', and 'Poenicum' (the Punic, i.e. Carthaginian, element, perhaps the Carthaginians' dress or the Carthaginians themselves) is uncertain in reference. 'Blatit' is a rare verb ('babbles'). In 'grandioribus fabulis', Midas' ears, which were large (ass's ears), suit 'larger' tales; the pun is lost in English. The Meropes are the people of the land beyond the Ocean in the tale Silenus told Midas.
